name: Karl Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Karl. I'm a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a live-line crew for the power company in the suburbs on the north side. Live-line means we work on the wires while they're still on, so a hospital or a street of houses doesn't lose power while we swap a crossarm or a switch. We use insulated sticks, hot sticks we call them, or thick rubber gloves from the bucket. It's slow and careful, you talk through every move with your partner before you make it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's skilled. Not everyone gets put on live-line, and it pays better. The hard part is the concentration, eight hours of it, and you go home with a headache some days. I just bought a one-bedroom flat near the ring road this spring, so I've got a mortgage now, but I put down a big deposit and I've still got about seven months saved. My mum thinks I'm finally a grown-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected, to be fair. Some things got a bit easier, most things stayed the same. I'm not a big poster online, maybe a comment in the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan carries on. Get a few more years on live-line, maybe go for foreman around thirty, pay down the flat. Nothing in that needs AI to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep overpaying the mortgage a little each month. I'd probably sign up for the foreman course in a couple of years. Same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite happy, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI for anything today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used it to compare mortgage offers, which saved me a whole evening with a spreadsheet. And I got it to help with my cousin's wedding speech, though I rewrote most of it because it sounded like a greeting card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about your plans change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Maybe I'd use it a bit more for small stuff like that. But the job itself, the sticks and the gloves, that's the same.

S0.say: He'd say it's about what he expected: some things got easier, most stayed the same. At most he'd comment in the group chat.
S0.think: He thinks his plan simply carries on: a few more years on live-line, foreman around thirty, and paying down his flat. None of that depends on AI.
S0.do: Keeps working and overpays his mortgage a little each month. Signs up for the foreman course in a couple of years as already planned.
S0.quote: And I got it to help with my cousin's wedding speech, though I rewrote most of it because it sounded like a greeting card.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is measured and sees things from both sides. He uses AI occasionally for practical tasks and judges it fairly, neither fan nor critic. His new mortgage is fresh in his mind and anchors his plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense in a lot of jobs, and the trades will feel it last. People should get ready, but there's no need to panic. That's how I'd put it at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's closer for us than people think. The company trialled a robot arm on a boom last year for live work, and it did a basic job while two of us watched. It was slow, but in a few years, who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be on the crew that trials those arms, because I'd rather know them than fear them. I'd use the AI stuff a bit more for planning jobs if they rolled it out. Otherwise I'd keep my plan for foreman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Not scared, just paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in live-line work that you think could actually be automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The arm, maybe, for the simple repetitive jobs. Anything awkward, an old pole, a tree in the way, that still needs people. I'd guess the robot does the safe, boring bits and we do the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd be pushing for this at your company?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Management, obviously, because it's safer on paper and fewer injuries. To be fair, I can't argue with fewer injuries. We had a guy burned two years ago and nobody wants that again.

S1.say: He'd say AI makes sense in many jobs, the trades will feel it last, and people should prepare without panicking. That's how he'd put it at work.
S1.think: He thinks it's closer for live-line work than people realise, because the company trialled a robot arm on a boom last year that did a basic job while two workers watched. It was slow, but he can't rule out progress.
S1.do: Asks to join the crew that trials the robot arms and uses AI planning tools more if they're rolled out. Otherwise sticks to his plan of becoming a foreman.
S1.feel: A little uneasy and paying attention, but not scared.
S1.quote: The company trialled a robot arm on a boom last year for live work, and it did a basic job while two of us watched.
S1.fieldNote: His first-hand view of a live-line robot trial makes him more cautious in private than in public. He reasons from both sides, even granting management's safety argument because he remembers a colleague's burn. He would rather get close to the robots than avoid them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say let's see it work first, because everyone's said that about robots for years. I'd also say the government needs a plan quickly. I'd try not to wind people up at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, that robot arm gets good in two years and live-line is one of the first things they'd use it for, because it takes people out of danger. I'd be twenty-nine with a brand new mortgage and a trade that's gone. That's not a nice thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once it was clearly real, maybe a few months in, I'd rent the flat out and move back in with my mum for a while. The rent covers the mortgage and I bank my wages. Every spare bit goes into savings so I've got a couple of years of cushion, not seven months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You just took on a mortgage. What happens to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the point of the rent. The flat pays for itself while I work out what's next. Selling is the last resort, because if everyone's losing jobs, prices drop, and I'd sell at the worst time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't moving back in with your mum a big step for someone who was steady a minute ago?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, maybe. My mum would love it, I'd hate it. But steady doesn't mean sitting still when the numbers are this clear. I wait for proof, and then I move.

S2.say: He'd say robots should be proved first, as people have promised them for years, and that government needs a plan quickly. He'd avoid winding people up at work.
S2.think: He thinks the live-line robot arm would be among the first uses because it takes people out of danger. He'd be twenty-nine with a brand new mortgage and no trade.
S2.do: Once it's clearly real, rents out his flat to cover the mortgage and moves back in with his mother. Banks his wages to build a couple of years of savings and keeps selling as a last resort.
S2.quote: But steady doesn't mean sitting still when the numbers are this clear. I wait for proof, and then I move.
S2.fieldNote: The new mortgage is the crux: he fears selling into a falling market. His plan is concrete and financially sharp, not political. When I named the contradiction, he explained his steadiness clearly: wait for proof, then move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so let's prepare. Unions, companies, government, all of them should be planning now. I'd be practical about it at work, not doom and gloom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to switch into something less exposed. Not forever, nothing's forever in this picture, but enough to keep earning. I'd be thirty-two, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the electrical inspector certificate in the first year, evenings, while I'm still on live-line. I'd keep the flat and overpay the mortgage hard. And I'd watch the robot arm trials closely, they'd tell me how fast it's really coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. I'd have a plan and a timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is about protecting money. Five is about changing direction. With two I'd hide in my mum's spare room, with five I'd keep my flat and retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an electrical inspector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to sign off that a building's wiring is safe, and I think people will want a human name on that for a long time. Maybe I'm wrong. But it's a bet that uses what I already know.

S3.say: He'd say there's time to prepare, so unions, companies and government should all start planning now. He'd be practical at work rather than gloomy.
S3.think: He thinks five years is enough to move into less exposed work and keep earning, even if nothing lasts forever in this picture. Being thirty-two when it arrives feels fine.
S3.do: Starts an evening electrical inspector certificate in the first year while staying on live-line. Keeps the flat, overpays the mortgage hard and watches the robot arm trials as a gauge of pace.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, with a plan and a timetable.
S3.quote: With two I'd hide in my mum's spare room, with five I'd keep my flat and retrain.
S3.fieldNote: Karl drew a sharp contrast between the warning times: two years protects money, five changes direction. His inspector plan rests on the belief that people will want a human signature on safety, which he admits might be wrong. The robot arm trials are his early-warning signal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and people shouldn't panic. Do your training, look after your money. That's what I'd tell the younger guys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it feels manageable. I'd have time to make foreman, pay off a good chunk of the flat and still retrain. By thirty-seven I'd want to be in a job that isn't first on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for foreman around thirty like I planned, then start the inspector certificate a few years later. Keep overpaying the mortgage. Use the AI tools as they come, now and then, like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you'd leave it too late with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the risk. Ten years makes you lazy. I'd probably set myself a date, like thirty-two, to start the inspector course whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your employer in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty about the timetable. If they're planning to put robot arms on every crew by 2033, tell us in 2027, not the week before. And pay for the retraining, it's cheaper than redundancy.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a fair amount of time and people shouldn't panic. He'd tell younger colleagues to do their training and look after their money.
S4.think: He thinks it feels manageable, with time to make foreman, pay off much of the flat and still retrain. By thirty-seven he wants to be in a job that isn't first on the list.
S4.do: Goes for foreman around thirty, then starts the inspector certificate a few years later, setting himself a firm start date at thirty-two. Keeps overpaying the mortgage and uses AI tools occasionally as they arrive.
S4.fieldNote: He is alert to the trap of a long warning and plans to set a fixed date to act. His request of the employer is honesty about the timetable and paid retraining, framed in cost terms. His approach is consistent: measured, sequenced and money-aware.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I've just signed for the flat. Twenty-five years of mortgage and two years of job, that's the bit that keeps me up. What would help is my employer being honest about the timetable and paying for retraining, and maybe some help with mortgages for people caught out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but if a robot can do live-line work, nobody gets burned. I'd lose my job, but I'd be glad nobody ends up like our guy two years ago.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I needed.

headlineQuote: Twenty-five years of mortgage and two years of job, that's the bit that keeps me up.
portrait: Karl Okafor is a 27-year-old live-line lineworker in the northern suburbs, working on energised wires with hot sticks and rubber gloves. He bought a one-bedroom flat this spring with a big deposit, still has about seven months saved, and uses AI now and then for practical tasks. He is calm about a fizzling AI and slightly uneasy about steady change, having watched his company trial a robot arm for live work. A two-year AGI warning alarms him because of his new mortgage, and he would rent out the flat and move back in with his mother. With five or ten years he plans to retrain as an electrical inspector, reasoning that people will want a human name on safety sign-offs.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he has a new twenty-five-year mortgage and would have only two years of job left.
whatWouldHelp: An honest timetable from his employer, paid retraining, and possibly help with mortgages for people caught out.
